solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Name of specific item

indicators.note: 'of' here means 'taken out of', so the letters come from inside the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters straddling the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A request to give the name of one particular object.
explanation.definitionFit: To cite something is to mention or quote it specifically, which is naming it as a verb.

clue.text: Ford repair makes one bad-tempered

parts.note: to ford a river is to cross it
to patch something is to mend it

explanation.surface: Fixing a Ford car leaves the mechanic in a foul mood.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital F makes Ford look like the car maker; it is the verb for wading across a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A crosspatch is an irritable, grumpy person, an old-fashioned noun for someone easily annoyed.

clue.text: Without drama, essay will restrict a new writer

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so the first word holds the rest inside it

parts.note: an essay is an attempt
taken as written
N is the standard abbreviation for new
a quill pen is a writing implement

explanation.surface: An essay calmly holding back a fresh author.
explanation.walkthrough: Essay here is the old sense of a try or attempt, not a piece of writing; the writer is the pen, not an author.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something tranquilly means calmly and peacefully, with no fuss or excitement involved.

clue.text: About to explode after removal of pin?

definitions.text: About to explode after removal of pin?

parts.words: About to explode after removal of pin?
parts.note: surface reading: a hand grenade primed once its safety pin is pulled
setter's reading: a person so furious they are ready to blow up with rage

explanation.surface: A grenade with its pin pulled, seconds from going off.
explanation.walkthrough: The grenade picture hides a person in a rage, ready to blow up at the slightest thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Being extremely angry is like being about to explode; the idiom pictures someone jumping with fury.

clue.text: Have zip that won't open

indicators.note: something that will not open has no opening, so the word loses its first letter

parts.note: zip is slang for nothing, zero

explanation.surface: Owning a zip fastener that is jammed shut.
explanation.walkthrough: Zip looks like a fastener but is the slang for zero; 'won't open' drops the front letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ought expresses obligation, as in 'you have to go', so it matches 'have' used before a verb.

clue.text: Reproduce, for piano, a passage

parts.note: pro means in favour of
p is the musical marking for piano, softly
taken as written
a gate is a way through

explanation.surface: Copying out a musical passage arranged for the piano.
explanation.walkthrough: Reproduce and passage suggest copying sheet music; reproduce is really the biological or horticultural sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To propagate plants or animals is to breed more of them, which is reproducing or multiplying them.

clue.text: Modified coal a recurrent source of power

indicators.note: modified means changed, so these letters are reworked into a new order

parts.note: the fodder letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Coal, once altered, becomes an energy source that keeps coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites thinking of coal itself as the power source; the whole phrase is just raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant splitting atoms produces heat to drive turbines, so it supplies electrical energy.

clue.text: Ape downs energy drink

indicators.note: to down something is to swallow it, so the first word takes the next one inside

parts.note: to go ape is to go crazy
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A monkey gulping an energy drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Ape looks like a noun but comes from the phrase 'go ape', meaning go crazy; 'energy drink' is split, energy giving its symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Mead is an ancient alcoholic beverage brewed from fermented honey and water.

clue.text: Man presumably coming to collect daughter

indicators.note: collecting someone means picking them up and holding them, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: due means expected to arrive
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A father who is supposedly on his way to pick up his daughter from school.
explanation.definitionFit: Dude is American slang for a guy or fellow, a casual word for any male.

clue.text: Bad luck to wind up senior academic

parts.note: vice is wickedness
chance is fortune

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to wind something is to roll it

explanation.surface: A run of misfortune ends up costing a university bigwig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind up' looks like a phrase meaning finish; here wind and up are separate, the second turning the first round.
explanation.definitionFit: In British universities the vice-chancellor is the chief executive, the most senior working academic administrator.

clue.text: Old mariner making a delivery

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a rating is an ordinary sailor in the navy

explanation.surface: The Ancient Mariner delivering something, perhaps cargo.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes Coleridge's ancient mariner and a parcel delivery; delivery here is the delivery of a speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Orating is giving a formal speech, and a speaker's manner of speaking is called their delivery.

clue.text: Source of fruit or veg

parts.note: taken as written
chard is a leafy green vegetable

explanation.surface: Where to get your fruit or vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchard is a plot planted with apple, pear or other trees grown for their crop.

clue.text: Take charge on extremely simple mission

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the word, its two end letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of simple
a quest is a search or mission
a rate is a fee or price charged

explanation.surface: Someone taking command of a very easy assignment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take charge' reads as one phrase but splits: take is the definition and charge is wordplay placed on (after) the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To sequestrate is to seize property legally, as a court confiscates assets pending a debt or dispute.

clue.text: Composer able to play with another? Fine

indicators.note: letters set to play are free to move around and rearrange themselves

parts.note: the fodder taken as written
another composer: Lionel Bart, who wrote the musical Oliver!
OK means all right

explanation.surface: A composer who can perform alongside a fellow musician, which is fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' refers back to the definition: another composer, Lionel Bart, the British songwriter of Oliver!
explanation.definitionFit: Bartók was a twentieth-century Hungarian who wrote orchestral, piano and chamber music.

clue.text: Indirectly, it keeps the clock ticking

definitions.meaning: first meaning: heard through someone else rather than first-hand
second meaning: the pointer that sweeps round once a minute

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a playful description; the pointer marking each passing tick on a clock face.
explanation.definitionFit: Information obtained via an intermediary is secondhand, and a clock's fastest pointer counts off seconds.

clue.text: Sort of early religious sect

parts.note: a.m. is the morning, early in the day
-ish is a suffix meaning roughly, sort of

explanation.surface: Describing a kind of primitive religious group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of early' reads as one phrase meaning primitive; the pieces are taken in reverse order.
explanation.definitionFit: The Amish are a traditionalist Christian community in America known for shunning modern technology.

clue.text: A deep breath?

parts.note: surface reading: a long lungful of air taken in
setter's reading: the deep is the ocean, and its breath is a light wind blowing off it

explanation.walkthrough: 'The deep' is a poetic name for the ocean, so its breath is wind coming off the water.
explanation.definitionFit: A gentle wind blowing in from the ocean toward the coast, poetically the exhalation of the waves.

clue.text: Port containers sent north with incense

indicators.note: in a down entry, going north means the word runs upwards, backwards

parts.note: vats are large tanks or vessels
to incense someone is to make them furious

explanation.surface: Shipping containers dispatched northward carrying fragrant incense.
explanation.walkthrough: Incense looks like the noun burnt in churches; it is the verb meaning to enrage.
explanation.definitionFit: Stavanger is a harbour city on the south-west coast of Norway, centre of its oil industry.

clue.text: Columns needing punctuation and edited English

parts.note: a colon is a punctuation mark

indicators.note: edited text has been reworked, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Newspaper columns that need proper punctuation and English editing.
explanation.walkthrough: Columns suggests newspaper articles to fit the editing theme, but it means pillars.
explanation.definitionFit: A colonnade is a row of pillars, usually supporting a roof, so the word names a set of columns.

clue.text: Muse over container's weight on return journey

indicators.note: a return journey goes back the way it came, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for over
tare is the weight of a container or vehicle without its load

explanation.surface: Pondering the weight of a shipping container on its way back.
explanation.walkthrough: Muse looks like a verb meaning ponder; it is a proper noun, one of the nine Greek goddesses.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is one of the nine Muses of Greek mythology, inspiring lyric and love poetry.

clue.text: It can secure cables and it's flexible

indicators.note: something flexible bends into new shapes, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Praise for a stretchy fastener that holds a bundle of cables together.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the answer, but only the opening words are the definition; the following words supply letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubber loop is stretched round things to hold them together, fastening them securely.

clue.text: They can secure money for the government, it's said

indicators.note: 'it's said' tells us to go by how the word is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: taxes are money levied by the state

explanation.surface: Government revenue that can secure a country's finances.
explanation.definitionFit: Small sharp nails or drawing pins fasten fabric or paper in place, so they hold things firmly.

clue.text: Musical instrument, gong, keeping its shape

indicators.note: keeping something means holding on to it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: gong is British slang for a medal or honour, here the Order of the British Empire
a medal is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: A gong being used as an instrument that holds its form.
explanation.walkthrough: Gong suggests the percussion instrument; in British slang it is an honour such as the OBE, and its round shape gives a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The oboe is a double-reed woodwind with a penetrating tone used in orchestras.

clue.text: Defeat right away

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
out means not at home, away

explanation.surface: Losing a match played away from home.
explanation.definitionFit: A rout is a crushing, decisive loss that sends the beaten side fleeing in disorder.

clue.text: Pirate in Merseyside port heading for Glasgow

parts.note: Bootle is a dock town on Merseyside, just north of Liverpool

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its front, so only its first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of Glasgow

explanation.surface: A buccaneer in a Liverpool-area port setting off for Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Pirate is the adjective or verb sense of illicit copying, not a seafarer, despite the port setting.
explanation.definitionFit: Bootleg goods are illegally made or copied, the same as pirated recordings or software.

clue.text: Spies crossing road, not quite the country

indicators.note: spies crossing something straddle it, so the first word goes around the others

parts.note: the CIA is the US intelligence agency

indicators.note: something not quite complete lacks its end, so the word before loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the

explanation.surface: Secret agents crossing a road near, but not quite in, some nation.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse is loose: road cut short gives three letters, and the extra letter has to come from the; American spies wrap around both.
explanation.definitionFit: Croatia is a nation on the Adriatic coast of south-east Europe, formerly part of Yugoslavia.

clue.text: To show initiative, draw on log

indicators.note: in an across clue, putting one thing on another places it after, so the first word named goes second

parts.note: to log something is to enter it in a record
to prise is to draw out or extract by force

explanation.surface: Showing resourcefulness by sketching on a piece of wood.
explanation.walkthrough: Draw and log suggest sketching on timber; both are verbs, the first placed on (after) the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Enterprise means readiness to undertake new projects, the quality of resourcefulness and drive.

clue.text: Son given child support for moving things

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
a kid is a child

explanation.surface: A boy receiving child benefit to help the family relocate.
explanation.walkthrough: Child support sounds like a payment; support is part of the definition instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A skid is a runner or plank placed under heavy loads so they can be slid along.
